claim: Electrostatic interactions between the NLRP3 polybasic (PB) region and negatively charged lipids on the trans-Golgi network (TGN) have been proposed to recruit NLRP3 to the TGN.
source: Electrostatic interactions between the NLRP3 polybasic (PB) region and negatively charged lipids on the trans-Golgi network (TGN) have been proposed to recruit NLRP3 to the TGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Chen and Chen, 2018) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Membrane association of NLRP3 is critically dependent on S-acylation of a highly conserved cysteine residue (Cys-130).
source: In this study, we demonstrate that membrane association of NLRP3 is critically dependant on S-acylation of a highly conserved cysteine residue (Cys-130), which traps NLRP3 in a dynamic S-acylation cycle at the Golgi
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including 2-BP treatment experiments (Figure 1F-G), mutation of Cys-130 (Figure 1H-I), and PEG-switch assays (Figure 4).

claim: S-acylation at Cys-130 traps NLRP3 in a dynamic S-acylation cycle at the Golgi.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that membrane association of NLRP3 is critically dependant on S-acylation of a highly conserved cysteine residue (Cys-130), which traps NLRP3 in a dynamic S-acylation cycle at the Golgi
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experiments showing dynamic membrane association (Figure 5E-G) and sensitivity to thioesterase inhibition (Figure 5A-D).

claim: A series of hydrophobic residues preceding Cys-130 act in conjunction with the PB region to facilitate Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that membrane association of NLRP3 is critically dependant on S-acylation of a highly conserved cysteine residue (Cys-130), which traps NLRP3 in a dynamic S-acylation cycle at the Golgi, and a series of hydrophobic residues preceding Cys-130 which act in conjunction with the PB region to facilitate Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments of hydrophobic residues (NLRP3HF mutant) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: NLRP3 becomes immobilised on the Golgi through reduced de-acylation of its Cys-130 lipid anchor following nigericin treatment.
source: Due to segregation from Golgi localised thioesterase enzymes caused by a nigericin induced breakdown in Golgi organisation and function, NLRP3 becomes immobilised on the Golgi through reduced de-acylation of its Cys-130 lipid anchor
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experiments showing reduced mobility after nigericin treatment (Figure 5F-G) and segregation of NLRP3 from APT2 (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Nigericin induces a breakdown in Golgi organisation and function that causes segregation of NLRP3 from Golgi localised thioesterase enzymes.
source: Due to segregation from Golgi localised thioesterase enzymes caused by a nigericin induced breakdown in Golgi organisation and function, NLRP3 becomes immobilised on the Golgi through reduced de-acylation of its Cys-130 lipid anchor
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing Golgi disorganization (Figure 6C-D) and impaired secretory trafficking (Figure 6C-F) after nigericin treatment.

claim: Disruptions in Golgi homeostasis are conveyed to NLRP3 through its acylation state.
source: Thus, our work defines a nigericin sensitive S-acylation cycle that gates access of NLRP3 to the Golgi.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing that nigericin-induced Golgi disruption correlates with changes in NLRP3 acylation dynamics.

claim: NLRP3 is an inflammasome seeding pattern recognition receptor activated in response to multiple danger signals which perturb intracellular homeostasis.
source: NLRP3 is an inflammasome seeding pattern recognition receptor activated in response to multiple danger signals which perturb intracellular homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Inflammasomes are multimolecular complexes that control the initiation of inflammatory responses to various damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: Inflammasomes are multimolecular complexes that control the initiation of inflammatory responses to various damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs; Chou et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Chou et al., 2023).

claim: NLRP3 is involved in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.
source: Due to its involvement in the pathogenesis of several diseases, including atherosclerosis (Duewell et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Heneka et al., 2013), one of the most well-studied inflammasome seeding PRRs is NLRP3
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Duewell et al., 2010).

claim: NLRP3 is involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Due to its involvement in the pathogenesis of several diseases, including atherosclerosis (Duewell et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Heneka et al., 2013), one of the most well-studied inflammasome seeding PRRs is NLRP3
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Heneka et al., 2013).

claim: Nigericin triggers canonical NLRP3 activation.
source: Stimuli that trigger canonical NLRP3 activation are diverse, ranging from bacterial ionophores such as nigericin (Perregaux et al., 1992) to agents which damage lysosomal integrity (Duewell et al., 2010; Hornung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Perregaux et al., 1992).

claim: Agents which damage lysosomal integrity trigger canonical NLRP3 activation.
source: Stimuli that trigger canonical NLRP3 activation are diverse, ranging from bacterial ionophores such as nigericin (Perregaux et al., 1992) to agents which damage lysosomal integrity (Duewell et al., 2010; Hornung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Duewell et al., 2010; Hornung et al., 2008).

claim: The majority of NLRP3 stimuli are unified by their ability to deplete intracellular potassium.
source: The majority of these stimuli are unified by their ability to deplete intracellular potassium, which has been proposed to be a common danger signal sensed by NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013).

claim: Depletion of intracellular potassium has been proposed to be a common danger signal sensed by NLRP3.
source: The majority of these stimuli are unified by their ability to deplete intracellular potassium, which has been proposed to be a common danger signal sensed by NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013).

claim: NLRP3 is a peripheral membrane protein recruited to the Golgi apparatus and endosomes through interactions between a highly conserved polybasic (PB) region within NLRP3 and negatively charged phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P).
source: Recent studies have revealed that NLRP3 is a peripheral membrane protein, recruited to the Golgi apparatus and endosomes through interactions between a highly conserved polybasic (PB) region within NLRP3 itself, and negatively charged phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P) found in the cytoplasmic leaflet of intracellular membranes (Chen and Chen, 2018; Lee et al., 2023; Schmacke et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chen and Chen, 2018; Lee et al., 2023; Schmacke et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).

claim: Membrane binding is important for formation of an inactive NLRP3 oligomer.
source: Membrane binding is important for formation of an inactive NLRP3 oligomer and an optimal response to NLRP3 stimuli (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018).

claim: Membrane binding is important for an optimal response to NLRP3 stimuli.
source: Membrane binding is important for formation of an inactive NLRP3 oligomer and an optimal response to NLRP3 stimuli (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018).

claim: Basic residues within the hyper-variable region (HVR) at the C terminus of K-Ras4B are paired with a proximal lipid anchor to confer specific localisation to the plasma membrane.
source: As one example directly relevant to NLRP3, basic residues within the hyper-variable region (HVR) at the C terminus of K-Ras4B, a membrane-bound GTPase that mediates key signalling events from the plasma membrane (Zhou et al., 2018), are paired with a proximal lipid anchor to confer specific localisation to the plasma membrane, with neither module alone sufficient for plasma membrane binding (Choy et al., 1999; Hancock et al., 1991; Hancock et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Choy et al., 1999; Hancock et al., 1991; Hancock et al., 1990).

claim: Neither the basic residues in the HVR nor the lipid anchor alone are sufficient for K-Ras4B plasma membrane binding.
source: As one example directly relevant to NLRP3, basic residues within the hyper-variable region (HVR) at the C terminus of K-Ras4B, a membrane-bound GTPase that mediates key signalling events from the plasma membrane (Zhou et al., 2018), are paired with a proximal lipid anchor to confer specific localisation to the plasma membrane, with neither module alone sufficient for plasma membrane binding (Choy et al., 1999; Hancock et al., 1991; Hancock et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Choy et al., 1999; Hancock et al., 1991; Hancock et al., 1990).

claim: The farnesyl group in K-Ras4B provides an initial non-specific weak affinity for all intracellular cellular membranes.
source: A working model for the steady state localisation of K-Ras4B at the plasma membrane posits that the farnesyl group provides an initial non-specific weak affinity for all intracellular cellular membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schmick et al., 2014; Yeung et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2017) as indicated in the following sentence.

claim: The PB region in K-Ras4B acts in concert with the farnesyl lipid anchor to allow K-Ras4B to preferentially partition to the plasma membrane through complementary charge-based interactions.
source: The PB region acts in concert with the farnesyl lipid anchor to allow K-Ras4B to preferentially partition to the plasma membrane through complementary charge-based interactions between the PB region and the high net negative charge of the plasma membrane imparted by the relative abundance of several species of negatively charged lipids (Schmick et al., 2014; Yeung et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schmick et al., 2014; Yeung et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2017).

claim: Golgi localised palmitoyl-acyltransferases (PATs) catalyse the addition of an acyl group to cysteine residues adjacent to the farnesylation motif at the C terminus of H-Ras and N-Ras.
source: For the farnesylated forms of H-Ras and N-Ras, Golgi localised palmitoyl-acyltransferases (PATs) catalyse the addition of an acyl group to cysteine residues adjacent to the farnesylation motif at the C terminus of H-Ras and N-Ras, trapping these proteins at the Golgi (Hancock et al., 1989; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Swarthout et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hancock et al., 1989; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Swarthout et al., 2005).

claim: S-acylation of H-Ras and N-Ras traps these proteins at the Golgi.
source: For the farnesylated forms of H-Ras and N-Ras, Golgi localised palmitoyl-acyltransferases (PATs) catalyse the addition of an acyl group to cysteine residues adjacent to the farnesylation motif at the C terminus of H-Ras and N-Ras, trapping these proteins at the Golgi (Hancock et al., 1989; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Swarthout et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hancock et al., 1989; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Swarthout et al., 2005).

claim: Thioesterase enzymes of the APT and ABHD families remove covalently attached acyl groups from S-acylated proteins.
source: The opposing action of thioesterase enzymes, such as those of the APT and ABHD families (Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Won et al., 2018), to remove covalently attached acyl groups helps to prevent the equilibration of S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins across all intracellular membranes through vesicular transport
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Won et al., 2018).

claim: Thioesterase activity helps to prevent the equilibration of S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins across all intracellular membranes through vesicular transport.
source: The opposing action of thioesterase enzymes, such as those of the APT and ABHD families (Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Won et al., 2018), to remove covalently attached acyl groups helps to prevent the equilibration of S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins across all intracellular membranes through vesicular transport, concentrating H-Ras and N-Ras at the Golgi and downstream compartments such as the plasma membrane (Dekker et al., 2010; Goodwin et al., 2005; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Salaun et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dekker et al., 2010; Goodwin et al., 2005; Rocks et al., 2010; Rocks et al., 2005; Salaun et al., 2010).

claim: Expression of GFP-NLRP3131-158 is insufficient to achieve Golgi localisation and predominantly localises to the nucleus.
source: Expression of GFP-NLRP3131-158 was insufficient to achieve a Golgi localisation however and predominantly localised to the nucleus (Figure 1B - top row, 3rd panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of GFP-NLRP3131-158-CVIM results in strong recruitment of GFP to the plasma membrane.
source: Similar to the charge biosensor probe +8 Pre (Eisenberg et al., 2021; Roy et al., 2000; Yeung et al., 2008), which is farnesylated and contains a PB region with a similar net positive charge to the NLRP3 PB region, expression of GFP-NLRP3131-158-CVIM resulted in strong recruitment of GFP to the plasma membrane (Figure 1B - middle row, 2nd and 3rd panels, quantified in Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in Figure 1C.

claim: Residues 131–158 within NLRP3 can act in conjunction with a second membrane binding signal to confer binding to specific intracellular membranes.
source: Thus, whilst the PB region alone is insufficient to drive association with intracellular membranes, residues 131–158 within NLRP3 can act in conjunction with a second membrane binding signal to confer binding to specific intracellular membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that GFP-NLRP3131-158-CVIM localizes to the plasma membrane (Figure 1B-C).

claim: Hydrophobic residues I113, W117, L120, L121, and L124 align along a single face of helix115-125.
source: Residues Tryp117, Leu120, Leu121, and Leu124 (labelled) align along a single face of helix115-125.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1E(ii).

claim: Treatment of cells with 2-bromopalmitate (2 BP) inhibits Golgi enrichment of NLRP3.
source: Golgi enrichment of NLRP3 in HeLaM cells transiently transfected with GFP-tagged NLRP3 was inhibited by treatment of cells with 2 BP (Figure 1F and G)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: 2-bromopalmitate (2 BP) is a palmitic acid analogue which blocks global protein S-acylation through covalent binding to the active site of ZDHHC enzymes.
source: To first determine if NLRP3 Golgi association was dependent on S-acylation, we treated cells with 2-bromopalmitate (2 BP), a palmitic acid analogue which is thought to block global protein S-acylation through covalent binding to the active site of ZDHHC enzymes (Davda et al., 2013; Jennings et al., 2009; Webb et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Davda et al., 2013; Jennings et al., 2009; Webb et al., 2000).

claim: 2 BP induced loss of NLRP3 from the Golgi is not due to alterations in Golgi PI4P levels.
source: 2 BP induced loss of NLRP3 from the Golgi was not due to alterations in Golgi PI4P levels, which remained similar in both untreated and 2BP-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 2 BP induced loss of NLRP3 from the Golgi is not due to an overall loss of Golgi integrity.
source: 2 BP induced loss of NLRP3 from the Golgi was not due to alterations in Golgi PI4P levels, which remained similar in both untreated and 2BP-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or due to an overall loss of Golgi integrity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: NLRP3 stimuli cause an increase in the recruitment of NLRP3 to intracellular membranes.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that NLRP3 stimuli cause an increase in the recruitment of NLRP3 to intracellular membranes, which have been proposed to represent either the Golgi (Chen and Chen, 2018) or endosomes (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chen and Chen, 2018; Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023).

claim: Nigericin treatment increases NLRP3 signal within the perinuclear area.
source: Consistent with these studies, we observed a similar increase in NLRP3 signal within the perinuclear area following nigericin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: The membranes NLRP3 resides on post-stimulation are likely derived from the Golgi.
source: The membranes NLRP3 resides on post-stimulation are likely derived from the Golgi as both GFP-NLRP3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C) and an untagged-NLRP3 construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) were sensitive to BrefeldinA (BFA), a Golgi disassembling fungal metabolite that has previously been shown to inhibit NLRP3 activation (Hong et al., 2019; Phulphagar et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by BFA sensitivity experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citations to prior work (Hong et al., 2019; Phulphagar et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: BFA treatment abolishes Golgi enrichment of NLRP3 at steady state.
source: BFA treatment abolished Golgi enrichment of NLRP3 at steady state and prevented accumulation of NLRP3 in the perinuclear region following nigericin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: BFA treatment prevents accumulation of NLRP3 in the perinuclear region following nigericin treatment.
source: BFA treatment abolished Golgi enrichment of NLRP3 at steady state and prevented accumulation of NLRP3 in the perinuclear region following nigericin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: 2BP treatment prevents the perinuclear clustering of NLRP3 signal observed following nigericin stimulation.
source: 2BP treatment prevented the perinuclear clustering of NLRP3 signal observed following nigericin stimulation and instead induced the formation of peripherally localised aggregates (Figure 1F and G)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi in response to nigericin is S-acylation dependent.
source: To test whether enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi in response to nigericin was dependent on S-acylation, we pre-treated cells with 2 BP overnight prior to a 1 hr stimulation with nigericin. 2BP treatment prevented the perinuclear clustering of NLRP3 signal observed following nigericin stimulation and instead induced the formation of peripherally localised aggregates (Figure 1F and G), indicating that enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi in response to NLRP3 stimuli is S-acylation dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by 2BP treatment experiments shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Mutation of Cys-130 prevents Golgi enrichment of GFP-NLRP3 at steady state.
source: In agreement with Cys-130 being a critical determinant of NLRP3 Golgi localisation, mutation of this residue phenocopied the effect of 2 BP, preventing Golgi enrichment of GFP-NLRP3 at steady state and in response to nigericin treatment (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Mutation of Cys-130 prevents Golgi enrichment of GFP-NLRP3 in response to nigericin treatment.
source: In agreement with Cys-130 being a critical determinant of NLRP3 Golgi localisation, mutation of this residue phenocopied the effect of 2 BP, preventing Golgi enrichment of GFP-NLRP3 at steady state and in response to nigericin treatment (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Mutation of hydrophobic residues I113, W117, L120, and L124 abolishes recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at steady state.
source: To test whether the hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 are also important for membrane binding we mutated residues isoleucine-113, tryptophan-117, leucine-120, and leucine-124 (hydrophobic face mutant; NLRP3HF), which are predicted to form a hydrophobic face as part of helix115-125 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, B). These mutations abolished recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at steady state and in response to nigericin (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C, D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C, D.

claim: Mutation of hydrophobic residues I113, W117, L120, and L124 abolishes recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi in response to nigericin.
source: To test whether the hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 are also important for membrane binding we mutated residues isoleucine-113, tryptophan-117, leucine-120, and leucine-124 (hydrophobic face mutant; NLRP3HF), which are predicted to form a hydrophobic face as part of helix115-125 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A, B). These mutations abolished recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at steady state and in response to nigericin (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C, D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C, D.

claim: Expression of NLRP395-130 localises predominantly to the cytoplasm with some Golgi enrichment visible.
source: In contrast, expression of residues 95–130 (NLRP395-130), containing both helix115-125 and Cys-130, localised predominantly to the cytoplasm with some Golgi enrichment visible, however this was not at levels similar to full length NLRP3 (Figure 1B – bottom row, 1st panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NLRP395-158 fails to recapitulate Golgi enrichment equivalent to the full-length protein.
source: Surprisingly, inclusion of the polybasic region (NLRP395-158) also failed to recapitulate Golgi enrichment equivalent to the full-length protein (Figure 1B – bottom row, 2nd panel), suggesting that additional features within NLRP3 are necessary to achieve recruitment to the Golgi.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NLRP395-158-CVIM achieves levels of Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment comparable to full length NLRP3.
source: Consistent with the need for an additional membrane affinity for maximal binding of NLRP3 to the Golgi, attachment of a C-terminal farnesylation sequence (CVIM) to NLRP395-158 (NLRP395-158-CVIM) was sufficient to achieve levels of Cys-130 dependent Golgi enrichment comparable to full length NLRP3 (Figure 1B, bottom row, 3d panel, quantified in Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in Figure 1C.

claim: Helix115-125, Cys-130 and the polybasic region are all essential for Golgi localisation.
source: Thus, whilst helix115-125, Cys-130 and the polybasic region are all essential for Golgi localisation, additional properties in NLRP3 are required to allow full Golgi binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments showing that disruption of any of these features impairs Golgi localization.

claim: Removal of the pyrin domain (PYD, residues 1–95) has no impact on Golgi localisation of NLRP3.
source: Removal of the pyrin domain (PYD, residues 1–95) had no impact on Golgi localisation; however, further truncation to residue 121 prevented association of NLRP3 with the Golgi in both untreated and nigericin treated cells, consistent with the requirement for an intact helix115-125 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–C, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–C, H.

claim: Truncation of NLRP3 to residue 121 prevents association of NLRP3 with the Golgi in both untreated and nigericin treated cells.
source: Removal of the pyrin domain (PYD, residues 1–95) had no impact on Golgi localisation; however, further truncation to residue 121 prevented association of NLRP3 with the Golgi in both untreated and nigericin treated cells, consistent with the requirement for an intact helix115-125 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–C, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A–C, H.

claim: NLRP31-699 localises to the Golgi at reduced levels compared to full-length NLRP3.
source: A C-terminal NLRP3 truncation lacking the LRR domain (NLRP31-699) localised to the Golgi at reduced levels, with further truncation down to residue 680 largely abolishing NLRP3 Golgi enrichment under both control and nigericin treated conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D–F, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8D–F, H.

claim: Truncation of NLRP3 to residue 680 largely abolishes NLRP3 Golgi enrichment under both control and nigericin treated conditions.
source: A C-terminal NLRP3 truncation lacking the LRR domain (NLRP31-699) localised to the Golgi at reduced levels, with further truncation down to residue 680 largely abolishing NLRP3 Golgi enrichment under both control and nigericin treated conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D–F, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8D–F, H.

claim: NLRP395-699 behaves the same as NLRP31-699.
source: Expression of a minimal NLRP3 construct spanning residues 95–699 (NLRP395-699) behaved the same as NLRP31-699, confirming that the LRR domain is important for optimal association of NLRP3 with the Golgi and that the PYD domain is dispensable (Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H.

claim: The LRR domain is important for optimal association of NLRP3 with the Golgi.
source: Expression of a minimal NLRP3 construct spanning residues 95–699 (NLRP395-699) behaved the same as NLRP31-699, confirming that the LRR domain is important for optimal association of NLRP3 with the Golgi and that the PYD domain is dispensable (Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H.

claim: The PYD domain is dispensable for NLRP3 Golgi association.
source: Expression of a minimal NLRP3 construct spanning residues 95–699 (NLRP395-699) behaved the same as NLRP31-699, confirming that the LRR domain is important for optimal association of NLRP3 with the Golgi and that the PYD domain is dispensable (Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8G, H.

claim: Overexpression of ZDHHC3 markedly enhances recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi.
source: Overexpression of the related enzymes ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 both markedly enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at the expense of cytosolic NLRP3 signal, with ZDHHC3 having a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Overexpression of ZDHHC7 markedly enhances recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi.
source: Overexpression of the related enzymes ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 both markedly enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at the expense of cytosolic NLRP3 signal, with ZDHHC3 having a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ZDHHC3 has a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
source: Overexpression of the related enzymes ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 both markedly enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi at the expense of cytosolic NLRP3 signal, with ZDHHC3 having a slightly stronger effect than ZDHHC7 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ZDHHC2, ZDHHC8 and ZDHHC9 weakly enhance NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
source: To a much weaker extent, ZDHHC2, ZDHHC8 and ZDHHC9 also enhanced NLRP3 Golgi recruitment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpression of ZDHHC5 causes NLRP3 to re-localise to the plasma membrane.
source: Unexpectedly, overexpression of the plasma membrane localised PAT ZDHHC5 decreased the amount of NLRP3 at the Golgi and instead caused NLRP3 to re-localise to the plasma membrane (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The effect of ZDHHC overexpression on NLRP3 localisation is dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
source: The effect of ZDHHC overexpression on NLRP3 localisation was dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzyme as catalytically inactive ZDHHC3C157S had no effect on recruitment on NLRP3 to the Golgi (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Cys-130 is essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
source: Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 were both essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment and the effect of ZDHHC5 on recruitment of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane as mutating either of these features prevented NLRP3 re-localisation in response to ZDHHC overexpression (Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claim: Hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 are essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment.
source: Cys-130 and hydrophobic residues within helix115-125 were both essential for the enhanced effect of ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 on NLRP3 Golgi recruitment and the effect of ZDHHC5 on recruitment of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane as mutating either of these features prevented NLRP3 re-localisation in response to ZDHHC overexpression (Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claim: Sensitivity to plasma membrane localised ZDHHC5 requires an intact PB region.
source: In agreement with the polybasic region driving affinity for highly charged membranes such as the plasma membrane and TGN (Eisenberg et al., 2021), sensitivity to PM localised ZDHHC5 required an intact PB region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cis-Golgi localised ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 when the PB region is mutated.
source: however, cis-Golgi localised ZDHHC3 (Ernst et al., 2018) was still able to recruit NLRP3 when the PB region was mutated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of interaction with intracellular membranes independent of the polybasic region.
source: These results suggest that helix115-125 and Cys-130 can drive low levels of interaction with intracellular membranes independent of the polybasic region, likely through the hydrophobic residues within helix115-125, but not at sufficient levels to show noticeable enrichment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ZDHHC3 can recruit NLRP3 with mutated PB region.

claim: Endogenous NLRP3 localises to the perinuclear region where it partially overlaps with the trans-Golgi marker p230 in THP-1 cells.
source: As previously described (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018), endogenous NLRP3 localised to the perinuclear region where it partially overlapped with the trans-Golgi marker p230 (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior work (Andreeva et al., 2021; Chen and Chen, 2018).

claim: Mutation of Cys-130 removes the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
source: Consistent with the requirement for Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues for Golgi localisation in HeLaM cells, mutation of these residues removed the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mutation of hydrophobic residues preceding Cys-130 removes the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
source: Consistent with the requirement for Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues for Golgi localisation in HeLaM cells, mutation of these residues removed the perinuclear pool of NLRP3 (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhances Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 in THP-1 cells.
source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S markedly enhances the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment in THP-1 cells.
source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E) and markedly enhanced the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment (Figure 3F and G)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Higher levels of ZDHHC3 activity can induce a greater percentage of cells to undergo NLRP3-dependent cell death.
source: Wild type but not catalytically inactive HA-ZDHHC3C157S enhanced Golgi recruitment of endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 3E) and markedly enhanced the percentage of cells positive for PI following nigericin treatment (Figure 3F and G), demonstrating that higher levels of ZDHHC3 activity can induce a greater percentage of cells to undergo NLRP3-dependent cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Labelling of S-acylated cysteines in NLRP3 reveals two bands indicative of singly and doubly S-acylated NLRP3 species in both HeLaM and THP1 cells.
source: Consistent with the presence of multiple cysteines in NLRP3 being S-acylated, labelling of S-acylated cysteines in NLRP3 revealed two bands indicative of singly and doubly S-acylated NLRP3 species in both HeLaM and THP1 cells (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: A large amount of NLRP3 remains resistant to hydroxylamine, suggesting a significant proportion of NLRP3 is not S-acylated at steady state.
source: A large amount of NLRP3 remained resistant to hydroxylamine, suggesting a significant proportion of NLRP3 is not S-acylated at steady state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Mutation of Cys-130 leads to only subtle changes in the S-acylation profile of NLRP3 with no loss of doubly S-acylated NLRP3.
source: Surprisingly, mutation of Cys-130 led to only subtle changes in the S-acylation profile of NLRP3 with no loss of doubly S-acylated NLRP3 (Figure 4A and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression correlates with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species.
source: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression and nigericin treatment both correlated with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species which did not occur when Cys-130 was mutated (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Nigericin treatment correlates with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species.
source: Enhanced NLRP3 Golgi binding driven by ZDHHC3 over-expression and nigericin treatment both correlated with an increased amount of a singly S-acylated wild type NLRP3 species which did not occur when Cys-130 was mutated (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: GFP-NLRP395-158 displays no mass shift following labelling of exposed S-acylated cysteines at steady state.
source: GFP-NLRP395-158 displayed no mass shift following labelling of exposed S-acylated cysteines and did not localise to the Golgi (Figure 4E–G), indicating that in the context of the small peptide used for this experiment, Cys-130 is not significantly S-acylated at steady state.
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: Overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increases enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi.
source: However, overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increased enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi (Figure 4E and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 induces a mass shift of NLRP395-158 following 5 kDa PEG maleimide labelling that is dependent on Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues.
source: However, overexpression of HA-ZDHHC3 significantly increased enrichment of NLRP395-158 at the Golgi (Figure 4E and F) and induced a mass shift of NLRP395-158 following 5 kDa PEG maleimide labelling that was dependent on Cys-130 and the preceding hydrophobic residues (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PEG-switch assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The linker region preceding the PB region is capable of undergoing S-acylation at Cys-130.
source: These results provide evidence that the linker region preceding the PB region is capable of undergoing S-acylation at Cys-130.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PEG-switch assay data showing Cys-130 dependent mass shift in NLRP395-158 upon ZDHHC3 overexpression (Figure 4G).

claim: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB causes loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi.
source: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB had a similar effect on NLRP3, with loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB causes re-localisation of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane, tubular recycling endosomes, and late endosomes.
source: Treatment of cells with PalmostatinB had a similar effect on NLRP3, with loss of NLRP3 signal at the Golgi (Figure 5A) and re-localisation of NLRP3 to the plasma membrane, tubular recycling endosomes, and late endosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 significantly reduces localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells.
source: Consistent with NLRP3 undergoing de-acylation, overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 (Abrami et al., 2021), but not mitochondrially localised APT1 (Kathayat et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), significantly reduced localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of mitochondrially localised APT1 does not significantly reduce localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells.
source: Consistent with NLRP3 undergoing de-acylation, overexpression of the Golgi localised thioesterase APT2 (Abrami et al., 2021), but not mitochondrially localised APT1 (Kathayat et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), significantly reduced localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi in unstimulated cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Overexpressed APT2 has no impact on Golgi morphology.
source: Overexpressed APT2 had no impact on Golgi morphology, indicating that loss of NLRP3 from Golgi membranes was not due to an effect of excess APT2 on Golgi integrity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–J.

claim: PalmostatinB treatment limits the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin.
source: Both PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression also limited the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin (Figure 5C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: APT2 overexpression limits the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin.
source: Both PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression also limited the accumulation of NLRP3 on the Golgi in response to nigericin (Figure 5C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Mitochondrial re-routing of APT2 from the Golgi prior to nigericin stimulation restores the enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi observed in response to nigericin.
source: The effect of APT2 overexpression appeared to be acute, suggestive of a direct action on NLRP3, as mitochondrial re-routing of APT2 from the Golgi prior to nigericin stimulation restored the enhanced recruitment of NLRP3 to the Golgi observed in response to nigericin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–G.

claim: NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle.
source: Thus, NLRP3 dynamically associates with intracellular membranes through an S-acylation cycle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined effects of PalmostatinB treatment and APT2 overexpression on NLRP3 localization.

claim: The kinetics of NLRP3 membrane binding in untreated cells are similar to those described for mono-S-acylated N-Ras with a half time to recovery of 58.4 s (±9.3 s S.D.).
source: The kinetics of NLRP3 membrane binding in untreated cells were similar to those described for mono-S-acylated N-Ras (Rocks et al., 2005) with a half time to recovery of 58.4 s (±9.3 ss S.D.), in agreement with NLRP3 rapidly cycling on and off the Golgi in an S-acylation cycle (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5E and F and citation to prior work (Rocks et al., 2005).

claim: Nigericin treatment suppresses the fluorescence recovery of NLRP3 after photobleaching.
source: Nigericin treatment suppressed the fluorescence recovery; whilst GFP-NLRP3 signal on average recovered to 75% of the pre-bleach signal in untreated cells, this was reduced to 44% after nigericin treatment, indicating that a greater fraction of NLRP3 that makes up the signal in the Golgi region is immobile following nigericin treatment (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A greater fraction of NLRP3 is immobile following nigericin treatment.
source: Nigericin treatment suppressed the fluorescence recovery; whilst GFP-NLRP3 signal on average recovered to 75% of the pre-bleach signal in untreated cells, this was reduced to 44% after nigericin treatment, indicating that a greater fraction of NLRP3 that makes up the signal in the Golgi region is immobile following nigericin treatment (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A proportion of perinuclear NLRP3 in nigericin treated cells remains resistant to rapamycin induced mitochondrial re-routing.
source: Reduced mobility of Golgi localised NLRP3 by FRAP was consistent with a mitochondrial re-routing assay using FKBP tagged GFP-NLRP3 where a proportion of perinuclear NLRP3 in nigericin treated cells remained resistant to rapamycin induced mitochondrial re-routing (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial re-routing assay data shown in Figure 5H, I.

claim: Changes in the membrane binding cycle of NLRP3 accompany its activation.
source: Changes in the membrane binding cycle of NLRP3 therefore accompany its activation, with less NLRP3 cycling off Golgi membranes following nigericin treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from FRAP and mitochondrial re-routing data showing reduced NLRP3 mobility after nigericin treatment.

claim: APT2 is tethered to the cytoplasmic face of the Golgi via S-acylation by the cis-Golgi localised PATs ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7.
source: The thioesterase enzyme APT2 is known to reside at the Golgi and is tethered to its cytoplasmic face via S-acylation by the cis-Golgi localised PATs ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC7 (Abrami et al., 2021; Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Ernst et al., 2018; Lin and Conibear, 2015; Vartak et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Abrami et al., 2021; Anwar and van der Goot, 2023; Ernst et al., 2018; Lin and Conibear, 2015; Vartak et al., 2014).

claim: In untreated cells, APT2S122A and NLRP3 signal are closely opposed.
source: In untreated cells, APT2S122A and NLRP3 signal were closely opposed (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: After nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulates on structures that are largely devoid of APT2S122A.
source: However, whilst some NLRP3 signal overlapped with APT2S122A after nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulated on structures that were largely devoid of APT2S122A (Figure 6A and B) indicating that APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
source: However, whilst some NLRP3 signal overlapped with APT2S122A after nigericin treatment, a large proportion of NLRP3 accumulated on structures that were largely devoid of APT2S122A (Figure 6A and B) indicating that APT2 becomes partially segregated from NLRP3 following nigericin treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Nigericin treatment induces dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi.
source: In contrast, nigericin treatment induced dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi (Figure 6C), as previously described (Chen and Chen, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and citation to prior work (Chen and Chen, 2018).

claim: Nigericin treatment induces a less pronounced dissociation of p230 positive trans-Golgi membranes from the cis / medial Golgi.
source: In contrast, nigericin treatment induced dissociation of TGN membranes (marked by TGN46) from the cis- and medial-Golgi (Figure 6C), as previously described (Chen and Chen, 2018), with a less pronounced dissociation of p230 positive trans-Golgi membranes from the cis / medial Golgi also observed (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Nigericin treatment leads to significant alterations in the organisation of distal Golgi cisternae relative to proximal cisternae.
source: Nigericin treatment therefore leads to significant alterations in the organisation of distal Golgi cisternae relative to proximal cisternae.
evidence: This claim is inferred from microscopy data showing dissociation of TGN and trans-Golgi from cis/medial Golgi (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin inhibits trafficking of FM4-hGH through the Golgi.
source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claim: Nigericin treatment has no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER.
source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claim: Golgi secretion and the flow of material beyond cis- and medial-Golgi cisternae is impaired by nigericin.
source: Nigericin treatment in the presence of rapamycin had no effect on exit of FM4-hGH from the ER, but inhibited its trafficking through the Golgi, with FM4-hGH accumulating in structures which overlapped with the cis/ medial Golgi marker STX5 (Figure 6C, D and F), demonstrating that Golgi secretion and the flow of material beyond cis- and medial-Golgi cisternae is impaired by nigericin.
evidence: This claim is supported by FM4-hGH trafficking data shown in Figure 6C, D and F.

claim: Disruptions to Golgi organisation and function caused by nigericin may limit the ability of APT2 to come into contact with NLRP3 and de-acylate it.
source: Thus, disruptions to Golgi organisation and function caused by nigericin may limit the ability of APT2 to come into contact with NLRP3 and de-acylate it (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of Golgi disorganization, impaired trafficking, and segregation of APT2 from NLRP3.

claim: Treatment of cells with monensin causes NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi.
source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H.

claim: Monensin does not activate NLRP3.
source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992).

claim: Monensin impairs Golgi function.
source: Enhanced Golgi recruitment of NLRP3 appears to be insufficient for NLRP3 activation however as treatment of cells with the Na+ selective ionophore monensin, which does not activate NLRP3 (Muñoz-Planillo et al., 2013; Perregaux et al., 1992), also caused NLRP3 to accumulate on the Golgi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and H) and impaired Golgi function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FM4-hGH trafficking data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The NLRP3 polybasic region alone is insufficient to achieve localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi.
source: NLRP3 Golgi binding has to date been shown to require interactions between the polybasic region of NLRP3 and PI4P (Chen and Chen, 2018). The NLRP3 polybasic region alone, however, is insufficient to achieve localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that GFP-NLRP3131-158 does not localize to the Golgi (Figure 1B).

claim: Electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction.
source: Similar to other peripheral membrane proteins that are S-acylated (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008), electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes provided by S-acylation at Cys-130 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and comparison to other S-acylated peripheral membrane proteins, supported by citations (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008).

claim: Stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes is provided by S-acylation at Cys-130.
source: Similar to other peripheral membrane proteins that are S-acylated (Chumpen Ramirez et al., 2020; Greaves et al., 2008), electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with intracellular membranes provided by the polybasic region and helix115-125 likely drive an initial low-affinity membrane interaction, with stable anchoring to and enrichment on Golgi membranes provided by S-acylation at Cys-130 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutation of Cys-130 prevents Golgi enrichment.

claim: Cys-130, helix115-125 and the polybasic region form a highly conserved functional unit that are essential for localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi apparatus.
source: Collectively, Cys-130, helix115-125 and the polybasic region form a highly conserved functional unit that are essential for localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi apparatus and potentially other intracellular membranes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined mutagenesis data showing that all three features are required for Golgi localization.

claim: LRR-dependent formation of an oligomeric NLRP3 complex may increase affinity for intracellular membranes through an avidity-based effect.
source: LRR-dependent formation of an oligomeric NLRP3 complex may therefore increase affinity for intracellular membranes through an avidity-based effect dependent on multiple monomers working together within a larger NLRP3 oligomer.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that the LRR domain enhances Golgi binding and from structural data showing polybasic regions organized around Cys-130.

claim: ZDHHC7 is responsible for NLRP3 S-acylation at Cys-130 in macrophages.
source: In agreement with our results showing that localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi can be controlled by the levels of ZDHHC3/7, a recent pre-print demonstrated that knockout of ZDHHC7 prevents localisation of NLRP3 to the Golgi and limits NLRP3 activation, suggesting that ZDHHC7 is responsible for NLRP3 S-acylation at Cys-130 in macrophages (Yu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent pre-print (Yu et al., 2023).

claim: Alterations in the levels of charged lipids on endosomes caused by NLRP3 stimuli could potentially allow NLRP3 to visit endosomal membranes and be trapped there by an endosomally localised PAT.
source: Alterations in the levels of charged lipids on endosomes caused by NLRP3 stimuli, as has previously been described (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), could potentially allow NLRP3 to visit endosomal membranes and be trapped there by an endosomally localised PAT.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from prior work (Lee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) and the authors' own data on ZDHHC5.

claim: Regulation of access to the Golgi through S-acylation at Cys-130 is likely to be important for oligomer formation.
source: Regulation of access to the Golgi through S-acylation at Cys-130 is likely to be important for oligomer formation and may represent another aspect of regulatory control over NLRP3 activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the known importance of membrane binding for oligomer formation and the authors' data on S-acylation.

claim: The steady state balance of S-acylation and de-acylation at Cys-130 may keep levels of Golgi localised NLRP3 below a critical threshold required for further NLRP3 oligomerisation or access to interaction partners and post translational modifications needed for optimal activation.
source: The steady state balance of S-acylation and de-acylation at Cys-130 may keep levels of Golgi localised NLRP3 below a critical threshold required for further NLRP3 oligomerisation or access to interaction partners and post translational modifications needed for optimal activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the authors' data on the S-acylation cycle.

claim: Deletion of residues 92–120 in mouse NLRP3 impairs IL1β release.
source: In mice, deletion of residues 92–120, which removes part of helix115-125, impairs IL1β release, with longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) completely removing Cys-130 and helix115-125 producing an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).

claim: Longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) in mouse NLRP3 that completely remove Cys-130 and helix115-125 produce an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation.
source: In mice, deletion of residues 92–120, which removes part of helix115-125, impairs IL1β release, with longer deletions (Δ92–132 and Δ92–148) completely removing Cys-130 and helix115-125 producing an even stronger reduction in inflammasome activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2021).

claim: Deletion of exon-3 (spanning residues 95–134) from human NLRP3 delays but does not completely block NLRP3 activation in human macrophages.
source: In contrast, deletion of exon-3 (spanning residues 95–134) from human NLRP3 delays but does not completely block NLRP3 activation in human macrophages (Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023).

claim: S-acylation at Cys-130 and binding to the Golgi may accelerate the process of inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to NLRP3 agonists.
source: In light of the latter study, S-acylation at Cys-130 and binding to the Golgi may accelerate the process of inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to NLRP3 agonists, although activation of human NLRP3 can still seemingly occur in the absence of Golgi binding.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that human NLRP3 can be activated without Golgi binding.

claim: Activation of human NLRP3 can still seemingly occur in the absence of Golgi binding.
source: In light of the latter study, S-acylation at Cys-130 and binding to the Golgi may accelerate the process of inflammasome formation or increase sensitivity to NLRP3 agonists, although activation of human NLRP3 can still seemingly occur in the absence of Golgi binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the study by Mateo-Tórtola et al., 2023 showing that deletion of exon-3 delays but does not block NLRP3 activation.
